Yes, plants can perceive and respond to sounds, as consistently reported across multiple credible sources. Research shows that plants exposed to caterpillar feeding vibrations produce more chemical defenses against herbivores, and can even distinguish these vibrations from other environmental sounds like wind [d3][d7]. Flowers have also been found to "hear" the buzz of approaching bees and respond within minutes by increasing the sugar content of their nectar by 12 to 20 percent [d6][d4][d5]. More broadly, plants perceive sound as a mechanical stimulus and translate it into cellular and metabolic changes, including altered gene transcription, changes in protein activity, and rearrangement of microfilaments [d1]. Plants also emit their own ultrasonic sounds, particularly under stress, suggesting a broader acoustic ecology involving both sound production and perception [d2].
